messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 64

He is twenty-seven, a journalist whose byline once carried weight in the city’s newsrooms. He works for a mid-sized daily, covering human-interest features and occasional investigations. Colleagues describe him as quiet, thorough, someone who used to volunteer for the toughest assignments. That was before.

It started two years ago, when he was still living with his ex-girlfriend. She was magnetic—a photographer who understood his late nights, his deadlines. At first, the intensity felt like passion. Then the first slap came during an argument about a missed call. He told himself it was an accident, her temper, his fault for pushing. The apologies were profuse, the tears real. He stayed.

Over the next year, the violence grew predictable: a shove in the kitchen, a punch to his ribs when he tried to leave the apartment, a hand around his throat during a fight about his work trips. He never went to a hospital. He never told his editor or his family. In his community, a man being hurt by a woman felt shameful, unthinkable. He was supposed to be strong, the provider, the one who protects. Instead, he became small. He stopped seeing friends. He stopped writing the deeper stories he loved—anything that required travel or risk felt like an invitation for her rage.

The end came when she broke his collarbone with a lamp. He drove himself to a clinic, lied about a fall down stairs, and then didn’t go home. That was eighteen months ago. He hasn’t spoken to her since.

Now he is in a new relationship, with a woman he met at a coffee shop. She is kind, patient, unaware of the full story. He has told her only that his last relationship was “bad.” He feels constant guilt: every time she raises her voice in playful frustration, he freezes. When she touches his arm unexpectedly, he flinches. He has started sleeping on the couch because his nightmares—quick flashes of the lamp, the sound of her heels on the tile—make him thrash and cry out. He wakes with his heart pounding, certain she is in the room.

His work has changed. He can no longer read police blotters or interview victims of domestic assault. His editor assigned him a piece on a shelter’s anniversary, and he developed chest tightness, nausea, and had to excuse himself to the bathroom. He typed a brief email requesting reassignment to food reviews and home décor. His editor, puzzled, agreed. He now avoids the newsroom on days when violence stories are discussed. He arrives early and leaves late, trying to stay invisible. His PCL-5 score is 64.

He drinks most nights—just enough to quiet the hypervigilance, to lower the volume of the memories that surface during quiet moments. He no longer runs, which used to be his release. The thought of being alone outside, at dusk, feels dangerous. He checks the locks three times before bed. He keeps his phone on silent. When his girlfriend asks what’s wrong, he says he’s tired, or he smiles and says nothing.

He has not told her about the nights he spent measuring doorways for escape routes, or how he sometimes still catches himself scanning a room for her, even though she lives in another state. He has not told her that when she touches his back in the dark, he sometimes sees a flash of that other hand, and has to bite his lip to stop from yelling. He wants to be close to her, but closeness feels like surrender. He wants to write again, but the sentences come out hollow. He wants to feel safe in his own skin, but that skin remembers.
